title: The Northern Seams
notebook: Two bids for the three closed iron mines of Halden Valley. Kessler-Tyvar offers capital and a year; the Ore Trust offers two years and a state loan.
Oskar Halm asked that the valley's own men be made foremen, not only labourers. Nobody in the room argued with him.
Vyktor: a Tyvaren foothold in Dravenhollow will be read as a foothold in the province, whatever the contract says.

narrative.text: The Mining Office in Halden Valley was built to house clerks who counted ore by the wagonload, and it still smells of wet timber and lamp oil. You reach it by the mountain road in the early afternoon, with Vyktor Reznik a step behind you and the valley falling away to the south. Three shafts stand on the slope above the town, their headframes grey against the pines. Below them the streets are quiet in the way of a place that has been waiting a long time to be asked a question.

The meeting room is cold, and someone has laid a fire that has not yet taken. A long table runs down the middle, with a map of the three mines pinned at one end. Dr. Ulrich Kessler stands beside it in a dark suit with a folder open at his elbow, and he has the composure of a man who rehearsed the first minute and found that it went well. Marta Ruzicka sits at the far side with her hands folded on a ledger. Oskar Halm has taken the chair nearest the door, his cap resting on his knee.

The Kessler-Tyvar Mining Consortium can have the three closed mines working within a year. We bring the capital, the pumps, the rail link to the border and the engineers to run them. We will hire from this valley first, and we will train the men who want to stay on the rock. The ore would travel north to Tyvaren foundries under an export agreement, which is the only reason the capital is willing to risk the shafts at all.

I want to be direct about one thing, Chancellor, because my government will ask me about it within the week. They are watching this decision closely. They would read a Veltrian contract as a sign of goodwill, and they would return that goodwill in trade and in the border crossings that have been closed for three years. I do not offer that as a condition. I mention it because you would want to know it before you decide.

The Veltrian Ore Trust can reopen one of the three shafts in about two years. We need a state loan to shore up the galleries and buy the pumps, and the loan is the whole of our capital. The ore stays in this country. It goes to the foundries at Kravenstal, where the steel for our rail and our shipyards is made, and every ton we sell is a ton that a Veltrian worker has helped to lift.

I know we are the smaller bid. Nobody in this room needs me to say it. But the Trust has never shipped ore it did not dig itself, and it will not promise ore to anyone who has not first been told how the galleries are being shored. That is slower than what Dr. Kessler is offering. It is also ours, and it will still be ours when the Consortium's government has changed its mind about the border.

Halm does not stand. He has the stillness of a man who spent thirty years underground and learned that the loudest voices are rarely the ones holding up the timber. He looks at the map for a while before he speaks, and when he does, the room adjusts itself around him. Kessler sets down his pen. Ruzicka looks up from the ledger for the first time since you came in.

The valleys have been dug by outsiders before. My father went down one of those shafts when it had another name, and the money left this valley on the same trains the ore came up on. Whoever wins this, hire Dravenni foremen, not only labourers. Give our people the timbering and the blasting and a voice in which galleries are safe to work. Then the money has somewhere to stay.

Nobody answers him. Kessler inclines his head as though he has been given a reasonable point and has no intention of arguing with it in front of you. Ruzicka looks at the table. Through the window the afternoon light lies flat across the slope, and somewhere down the valley a train whistles at the border line and then falls silent again.

The Tyvaren bid is the faster road, and I will not pretend the thaw is worth nothing. The border has been shut for three years, and the trade has gone with it. The Consortium's money would be in the valley within the season, and the Tyvaren government would take that as a reason to talk to us. But it would also put a foreign company, with a foreign government's attention, into the most sensitive province we have. The Dravenni will read every shaft Kessler opens as a border post.

The Trust is honest and cannot finish the work. The Consortium can finish it and would own the result. Halm asked for one thing, a fair share of his own valley, and it is the one request in this room that nobody has yet offered to meet. Turn the map a few degrees toward you and ask which of the three answers you could still defend to the people in this room a year from now, when the first shaft is either working or it is not.

There is a middle road that neither bidder has offered in full. The Republic can enter a joint venture with the Consortium, taking a state share in the mining company and a seat on its board. The money comes in, the controls stay partly in Veltrian hands, and the Republic becomes a partner in a foreign-capitalised mine in the province the Assembly least wants to see one. That is the price of it, and it will be the first thing the Dravenni deputies ask about.

monologue: Two bids, three shafts, and a valley that has heard promises before. Kessler offers speed and foreign money, with a border that might open in return. Ruzicka offers a slower restart that stays in Veltrian hands. Vyktor has laid out a state partnership that brings money and keeps a hand on the controls, and he has not said which way he would go.

choices.text: "Award the concession to the Kessler-Tyvar Consortium. The valley needs work before winter, and the border has been shut too long. We will hold them to the one-year timetable and the hiring terms in writing."

reactions.text: Halm puts his cap back on, slowly, and stands. He does not argue. He says he will be at the first meeting with the foremen, and that he intends to count them.

Tyvaren will call this a thaw and Kravenstal will call it a surrender, and both will be partly right. The valley will remember that it was not asked first, and that memory will outlast the first year of wages.

choices.text: "Award the Veltrian Ore Trust the state loan and the one shaft. It will be slow, and the ore will be ours. The foundries at Kravenstal get the work, and the valley gets wages it can count on."

reactions.text: Ruzicka closes the ledger. She does not thank you. She says the Trust will need the loan in this budget and not the next, and she says it while looking at Vyktor rather than at you.
A loan of that size is a Treasury line before it is an Assembly motion. The Consortium will say the Republic chose sentiment over capital, and the Tyvaren press will say it louder. Be ready for both.

choices.text: "Award the concession to the Kessler-Tyvar Consortium, and the Republic takes a state share and a seat on the board. We keep the money and a hand on the controls. We pay for it with debt we will have to carry."

reactions.text: Kessler accepts the terms with the ease of a man who expected to be asked for more. He says his board will want the state share in writing, and then asks, very courteously, which ministry will be signing for it.

A state share makes the Republic answerable for every shaft that goes wrong. You are buying control, and you are buying the blame with it, and the Assembly will want to know which of the two you were paying for.

choices.text: "Reject both bids for now. Ask the Mining Office for a full survey of the three shafts, and bring both proposals back when we know what the rock is worth. Neither is ready to sign."

reactions.text: Halm nods once. He says a survey is a thing the valley has been promised before, and that he will stand at the mouth of the first shaft when it is done, whoever is holding the paperwork.

Vyktor writes the instruction without comment and closes his pad. He does not say that the Consortium's government will read the refusal as a closed door, or that the Trust will spend the winter waiting. He has already drafted both letters.
